section_summary: This section records Allied objections to a third Japanese Antarctic whaling expedition in 1948–49 and the U.S. decision to support an expedition limited to two factory ships. It also covers disputes over Japanese fishing boundaries, a proposed Japanese fishery patrol near China, and the treatment of vessels fishing outside authorized areas. The final pages document SCAP’s authorization of the whaling expedition.

subfiles.title: Conclusion of memorandum of conversation on Australian reactions
subfiles.about: Australia questions SCAP actions on bauxite and fishing and seeks further Allied consultation.
subfiles.summary: Concludes an earlier copy of the Makin–Saltzman conversation.

subfiles.title: Australian Reaction to Matters within the Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: Australian Ambassador Makin challenges SCAP’s decisions on whaling and other matters before the Far Eastern Commission.
subfiles.summary: Makin objects to a third whaling factory ship, criticizes treatment of an Australian observer, and questions unilateral SCAP action on coastal patrols, Japanese travel, and bauxite imports. Saltzman defends SCAP’s authority while promising further consultation.

subfiles.title: Aide-Memoire to Australian Ambassador
subfiles.about: Snow evaluates the legal basis for SCAP action absent a Far Eastern Commission policy decision.
subfiles.summary: Snow argues that SCAP has broad power to act until constrained by an FEC decision. He considers the proposed U.S. reply’s reliance on occupation necessity unduly narrow.

subfiles.title: SCAP’s Authority to Act in the Absence of Policy Basis
subfiles.about: Claxton requests legal review of SCAP’s powers where no applicable policy exists.
subfiles.summary: Requests careful review of a disputed passage in the proposed reply to Australia.

subfiles.title: New Zealand response on Japanese Antarctic whaling
subfiles.about: New Zealand accepts another expedition but questions a third factory ship and seeks FEC consideration.
subfiles.summary: Seeks route details and a regular FEC decision on Japanese whaling.

subfiles.title: U.S. reply to New Zealand on the third whaling expedition
subfiles.about: The United States reports SCAP’s decision to authorize another expedition with two factory ships.
subfiles.summary: Cites Japan’s food shortage and foreign exchange needs, explains the decision against adding a third ship, and maintains SCAP’s authority to authorize the expedition.

subfiles.title: United Press request for information relative to Japanese whaling
subfiles.about: United Press asks about the planned Japanese expedition, foreign consultations, and observers.
subfiles.summary: Officials confirm SCAP’s intention to authorize a 1948–49 expedition and identify governments notified and observers aboard earlier vessels.

subfiles.title: Norwegian protest against continued Japanese Antarctic whaling
subfiles.about: Norway formally protests Japanese participation in Antarctic whaling.
subfiles.summary: Norway argues that the fixed catch quota means Japanese vessels reduce Allied catches without increasing overall oil production. It stresses investments in rebuilding its fleet, concern about declining blue whales, and the whaling industry’s importance to Norwegian recovery. It offers to sell whale meat for Japan.

subfiles.title: U.S. reply to Norwegian whaling protest
subfiles.about: The United States explains why SCAP authorized another expedition despite Norway’s protest.
subfiles.summary: The reply cites Japanese food and foreign exchange needs, acknowledges Norway’s economic concerns, and emphasizes that SCAP rejected a third factory ship.

subfiles.title: British objections to Japanese Antarctic whaling
subfiles.about: Britain opposes another Japanese expedition and requests a Far Eastern Commission decision.
subfiles.summary: Britain questions Japan’s food and oil needs, argues that Japanese catches and exports damage Allied whaling economies, and warns against prejudging peace treaty terms. It especially objects to expanding the expedition to three factory ships.

subfiles.title: Japanese Whaling
subfiles.about: British diplomats explain their objections to SCAP’s proposed third Japanese factory ship.
subfiles.summary: Balfour and Graves stress British and Norwegian wartime fleet losses and the effect of Japanese catches on Allied quotas. Armour says Japan should not face restrictions solely for being a former enemy and promises to relay their views to SCAP.

subfiles.title: U.S. reply to British objections
subfiles.about: The United States reports SCAP’s two-fleet decision and restates its position on SCAP authority.
subfiles.summary: The reply cites Japan’s food and import needs, refers Britain to earlier statements on FEC jurisdiction and whaling policy, and hopes limiting the expedition to two factory vessels addresses some objections.

subfiles.title: Duplicate memorandum of conversation on Japanese whaling
subfiles.about: A degraded copy records the British conversation about Japanese whaling.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate of the May 19 Balfour–Armour conversation.

subfiles.title: Duplicate British aide-mémoire on Japanese whaling
subfiles.about: A degraded copy repeats Britain’s objections to the proposed expedition.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate of the British May 18 aide-mémoire.

subfiles.title: Dispatch of Attached Telegram re Third Whaling Expedition
subfiles.about: Allison argues against issuing a U.S. interim directive authorizing the third expedition.
subfiles.summary: He holds that SCAP can act without an FEC policy decision and that an interim directive lacks a sound urgency basis, shifts responsibility needlessly, and could imply earlier authorization was improper.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Norwegian Ambassador
subfiles.about: Butterworth forwards his conversation with Norway’s ambassador for possible notice to the Secretary.
subfiles.summary: Suggests bringing the conversation’s final paragraph to the Secretary’s attention.

subfiles.title: Japanese Whaling
subfiles.about: Norway’s ambassador reiterates opposition to the projected Japanese Antarctic expedition.
subfiles.summary: Munthe de Morgenstierne describes Norway’s fleet investment, limited catch quota, and dependence on whaling revenue. Butterworth promises to inform Secretary Marshall of Norway’s concern.

subfiles.title: Copy of Norwegian whaling protest
subfiles.about: An enclosed copy repeats Norway’s formal protest against Japanese Antarctic whaling.
subfiles.summary: The copy recounts prewar whaling regulation, Norway’s fleet reconstruction, the catch quota, and its offer to supply whale meat to Japan.

subfiles.title: Northward Extension of Japanese Fishing Area
subfiles.about: Sebald reports rejection of a proposed northward expansion of Japanese fishing waters.
subfiles.summary: Forwards a staff study and says the proposal may be reconsidered after FEC discussions.

subfiles.title: Northward extension of the authorized fishing area
subfiles.about: The Natural Resources Section proposes moving the northern Japanese fishing boundary.
subfiles.summary: The study says the boundary near Hokkaido creates navigation hazards, restricts traditional crab grounds, and concentrates fishing effort. It recommends a revised line while asserting that Soviet interests would be little affected.

subfiles.title: Anti-Japanese feeling over reported fishing in Chinese waters
subfiles.about: The fragment concerns reports of Japanese fishing vessels in Chinese waters.
subfiles.summary: Poor OCR preserves only the subject and a denial of a reported charge.

subfiles.title: Plan for Japanese Fishery Patrol in the East China Sea
subfiles.about: Sebald reports opposition within SCAP headquarters to a proposed Japanese patrol.
subfiles.summary: The despatch explains persistent violations of fishing limits, weak evidence in Japanese prosecutions, Korean confiscations, and threatened Chinese measures. Sebald’s Diplomatic Section opposes the patrol and asserts SCAP’s authority over violations on the high seas.

subfiles.title: Japanese fishery patrol in the East China and Yellow Seas
subfiles.about: The Natural Resources Section recommends a Japanese vessel to monitor fishing-limit violations.
subfiles.summary: The study proposes using Hatsutaka-Maru to identify violators and gather evidence admissible in Japanese courts, with limits on its approach to foreign coasts.

subfiles.title: Authorized Japanese Fishery Patrol in East China and Yellow Seas
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: A draft directive would authorize a named Japanese patrol vessel under geographic restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Authorizes a patrol, reporting requirements, and a coastal exclusion zone; disclaims any decision on territorial rights.

subfiles.title: Diplomatic Section objections to Japanese fishery patrol
subfiles.about: The Diplomatic Section rejects the proposed patrol on political and practical grounds.
subfiles.summary: It predicts Chinese objections and reprisals, possible damage to fishing-area negotiations, and little benefit from one vessel. It also argues that China should report high-seas violations to SCAP rather than punish them itself.

subfiles.title: Japanese Fishing Craft in Unauthorised Waters
subfiles.to: U.S. Army Military Government in Korea distribution
subfiles.about: Korean authorities are directed to apprehend Japanese fishing craft in restricted waters.
subfiles.summary: Provides for provost court trials, vessel confiscation after conviction, and crew deportation.

subfiles.title: Chinese warning about Japanese fishing outside authorized areas
subfiles.about: China warns that it may act unless Japanese fishing violations stop.
subfiles.summary: Acknowledges GHQ’s inquiries but reports continuing violations and threatens appropriate measures.

subfiles.title: China Navy Sinks Japanese Vessel
subfiles.about: A press report describes Chinese naval action against Japanese fishing boats.
subfiles.summary: Reports one vessel sunk, another captured near the Yangtze, and 25 Japanese detained.

subfiles.title: Airgram endorsing opposition to Japanese fishery patrol
subfiles.about: The State Department supports Sebald’s objections to the proposed patrol.
subfiles.summary: Asks Sebald to discourage any revived proposal and report developments.

subfiles.title: Handwritten routing comments on proposed patrol airgram
subfiles.about: Officers recommend informing Sebald of Department support and continuing to oppose the patrol.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten comments propose an airgram backing Sebald’s position; a reviewer agrees and requests a draft.

subfiles.title: Attached Despatch
subfiles.about: Green summarizes Sebald’s despatch and endorses opposition to the proposed Japanese patrol.
subfiles.summary: He reviews the patrol plan, Chinese and Korean enforcement concerns, and the Diplomatic Section’s objections. He considers a Japanese patrol near China politically harmful and ineffective.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning purchase of Japanese fish on the high seas
subfiles.about: The Department directs Holm’s proposed fish-purchase questions to SCAP and U.S. Customs.
subfiles.summary: Explains that SCAP controls Japanese fishing and Customs must determine the cargo’s eligibility for entry.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about buying Japanese fish for processing in Hawaii
subfiles.about: Holm asks whether his company can buy Japanese-caught fish at sea for canning in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Seeks advice on U.S. law and SCAP restrictions for transfers on the high seas.

subfiles.title: Personal letter on the whaling expedition and Tokyo staffing
subfiles.about: Sebald reports progress on the two-ship expedition and discusses UNTCOK and staffing.
subfiles.summary: Says the expedition is proceeding with two factory ships, describes Drumright’s arrival, and raises his need for assistance and consultation in Washington.

subfiles.title: Reply to Sebald on whaling and UNTCOK
subfiles.about: Butterworth welcomes the two-ship decision and explains State–Army exchanges about UNTCOK accommodation.
subfiles.summary: He expects limiting the whaling expedition to ease Allied objections. He then recounts how Army officials and Secretary Marshall sought accommodation in Tokyo for the U.N. Temporary Commission on Korea.

subfiles.title: Request for accommodation for the U.N. Temporary Commission on Korea
subfiles.about: Marshall requests quarters in Tokyo for UNTCOK members preparing their report.
subfiles.summary: Asks Royall to direct MacArthur to provide accommodation.

subfiles.title: Authorization of Japanese Antarctic Whaling Expedition for the 1948–1949 Season
subfiles.about: Sebald forwards SCAP’s whaling authorization and an earlier staff study.
subfiles.summary: The despatch states that SCAPIN 1913 authorizes two fleets, substantially following the preceding season’s terms. It explains that an earlier three-fleet proposal was reduced after consultation and strong foreign objections.

subfiles.title: Japanese Whaling Operations in the Antarctic in the 1948–1949 Season
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: SCAP authorizes a two-fleet Antarctic whaling expedition under international rules.
subfiles.summary: Requires Japan to submit a detailed operational plan and obtain approval for later vessel or personnel substitutions.
